sections.title: What description covers
sections.intro: Today's law sets how dense description is and almost nothing about how wide it ranges, so the page keeps returning to bodies, rooms, papers and wounds. These questions set which subjects a thread must keep reaching for, and whose eye picks them out.

questions.title: How wide description must range
questions.question: Should the range of subjects a scene describes become law, and in what shape?
questions.context: R48-02 asks for 'Lush throughout' and R51-31 sends scenes to the sense bank first, but nothing sets how widely description ranges, and the archive leans on bodies, rooms, documents and wounds. Chinese and Japanese prose rotate through landscape, season and household; the Victorian novel ranges across money, streets and institutions.

options.label: Range by ear (current)
options.consequence: No range rule. Lush density (R48-02) and the sense bank first (R51-31) stand, and Natalie widens by judgement. Nothing new is checked.
options.sample: The quartermaster's store smelled of seal fat and wet felt. Hob Varley stamped the snow off his boots at the door and waited while the man behind the trestle finished his count. He was broad and grey at the temples, his knuckles split by the cold and greased against it. A blubber lamp spat on the shelf above his head. Even indoors his breath stood white in front of his face. "Courier," he said, without looking up. "How's your stack?" Hob had no stack. He had a satchel of Hallenfeld paper and two feet he could no longer feel.

options.label: Lead plus two, thread-checked
options.consequence: Each scene brief names one lead subject group and two supporting groups; the lead changes from scene to scene, and session end lists any group untouched for four scenes.
options.sample: Salt bought a bench and broth at the quartermaster's store, and Hob Varley had brought Accord silver, which nobody north of the arrays would take. He gave a carter two marks for one gritty bar and knew he had been robbed. Outside the door a boy was splitting rounds for the woodpile, setting each on the block with its checks toward him so the axe found the crack and the halves fell clean. The aurora had come up green over the grey rock of the Seat. The quartermaster scraped the bar with a thumbnail to see it was salt all through, and let him in.

options.label: Five groups every scene
options.consequence: Every scene or full turn touches at least five subject groups, one of them from the thin list. The widest page, with some risk of reading as a survey.
options.sample: Snow came sideways off the rock as Hob Varley reached the outer town, and above the Seat the aurora stood in two green folds. Six hundred men were breathing in the yard, waiting on the broth. A woman ladled it, and the first bowl went to an old rider whose hands had gone in the Thin Weeks; she held it to his mouth herself. A boy split rounds and stacked them pale ends outward. The quartermaster took Hob's salt and scraped it with a thumbnail. He gave him a bench with a chip of night-stone under the blanket, for the fever, the boy said.

options.label: Thread count only
options.consequence: Scenes stay free. Session end lists every group untouched for four scenes, and the next scene brief must draw on them.
options.sample: Hob Varley came in along the horse lines, where the Seat kept its riding stock under hide awnings: steppe horses gone shaggy for the winter, frost knotted in their manes, a grey mare standing hipshot with her eyes half shut and one ear turned to him. Moss showed black where the wind had scoured the snow off the rock, the only growing thing for a day's ride. Dung steamed in the cold. The quartermaster's store stood at the end of the lines, and the seal fat reached him before he found the door.

questions.rec_reason: It turns your ask into something a brief can carry without a quota feeling: one subject the scene is built around, two more at its edges, and a check across the thread so nothing goes dark for long.

questions.title: The world outside the walls
questions.question: Which of these subject groups join the rotation a thread must keep returning to?
questions.context: No Inventory has a land, sky, plant or animal field, and the archive sees landscape through windows: plants come up about 0.5 times per 1,000 words, and the moon and stars never reach the page. Chinese shanshui (mountain-and-water painting) and Japanese season poetry put this group first; Tolkien walks the road and names the ground.

options.label: Land, water and sky
options.consequence: Terrain and ground underfoot, rivers, sea and shore, the horizon, and the night sky (Shiro the moon, the five wanderers, the Nail, the aurora) join the rotation.

options.label: Plants and animals
options.consequence: Trees, crops, herbs, blossom, birds, insects, working beasts and Well-spawn as creatures to be looked at join the rotation.

options.label: Seasons and weather
options.consequence: Thaw, rain, heat, fog and the signs of each culture's turning of the year join the rotation, on top of R53-09's actual weather in every outdoor scene.

options.label: History in layers
options.consequence: Ruins, re-used stone, a road over an older road, heirlooms, and the Gone lists made visible as things in the world join the rotation.

questions.rec_reason: All four are thin on the page, and they are what the Eastern half of the blend sees first; a thread that never looks up at the sky or down at the moss is missing half its world.

questions.title: The made world
questions.question: Which of these subject groups join the rotation a thread must keep returning to?
questions.context: Interiors and Draw Age machinery run heavy; architecture as style, dress after first sight, and streets and crowds run thin (crowds about 0.3 per 1,000 words). R59-07 and R59-08 already set the Victorian city and class-layered dress. Dickens reads a city whole; the Japanese war tale reads rank in armour lacing and sleeve colour.

options.label: Architecture as style
options.consequence: Buildings are described for their style and ornament as well as their use and wear; the Moto 'one thing made that serves no function' finally gets looked at.

options.label: Draw Age machinery
options.consequence: Standpipes, gauge-housings, conduit, meters, rail, lifts, lamps, the draw-hum and the silence of a cut district join the rotation.

options.label: Dress and fabric
options.consequence: Cloth, cut, colour by rank, wear and repair, adornment and worn scent join the rotation, past the first-sight inventory.

options.label: Streets and crowds
options.consequence: Squares, alleys, hawkers, the rich quarter and the tenement, and the crowd as one body join the rotation.

questions.rec_reason: Dress and streets are where class shows without a word, and the machinery is the period's signature; architecture as style is the one subject the Moto Inventory already asks for that nobody has looked at.

questions.title: The working world
questions.question: Which of these subject groups join the rotation a thread must keep returning to?
questions.context: Money and records are steady in the archive. Craft is named more than shown, food is a prop and rarely tasted, and courts and punishment have no Inventory field though R53-11 and R60-21 say they belong there. Dream of the Red Chamber and Martin spend pages on the table; O'Brian and the master-craftsman story spend them on work.

options.label: Craft and labour
options.consequence: Work as process, tools and workshops, guild marks, apprenticeship, the body a trade makes, and dying trades join the rotation.

options.label: Money, prices, markets
options.consequence: Coin and its weight, prices called and paid, wages, stalls and haggling, branded goods (R60-07), debt and the bill join the rotation.

options.label: Food and the table
options.consequence: Ingredients, cooking, the meal as rite, hunger and rationing, drink, street food and taste in the mouth join the rotation.

options.label: Rank, law and records
options.consequence: Precedence and titles in a room, seals and signatures, courts and punishments, registers, maps and handwriting join the rotation.

questions.rec_reason: This is where money comes before magic (R53-17) and where rank lives in a room, and taste and craft are the two things the archive most underuses.

questions.title: Rite, play and the household
questions.question: Which of these subject groups join the rotation a thread must keep returning to?
questions.context: No festival has reached the page, no instrument, game or toy is attested for any culture, and children and the rich are nearly absent. R59-15 already licenses theatre, music hall, sport and fairs. Pansori (Korean sung storytelling), Genji's court arts and Peake's rituals make this group the texture of a world.

options.label: Rites, festivals, the dead
options.consequence: Rites performed on the page, shrines and household observance, funerals and mourning, festivals and folk taboos acted on join the rotation.

options.label: Music, art and play
options.consequence: Instruments and songs, carving and painting, theatre and storytellers, games of chance and skill, sport and toys join the rotation.

options.label: Households, rich and poor
options.consequence: Servants and the order of a house, who sleeps where, and how the rich live at home as well as the poor join the rotation.

options.label: Children and the old
options.consequence: The child's world (its games, chores, fears and lessons) and old age (its place at the fire, its work, its body) join the rotation.

questions.rec_reason: A world with no song, no game and no festival reads as all work and grief, and grimdark lands harder once the reader has seen what there was to lose.

questions.title: Culture-keyed noticing
questions.question: Should a culture decide what a description notices, and whose culture: the viewer's, the place's, or both?
questions.context: No rule keys what a POV notices to culture; R48-04 keys only metaphor, to 'the POV's own life'. Tanizaki reads a Japanese room through shadow and lacquer; the Victorian novel reads one through price. The Inventories already imply each eye: Moto accuracy, Accord weight and seal, Kharven scarcity. A mixed room (R53-23) puts two eyes in one place.

options.label: Plain sensory eye (current)
options.consequence: Rooms are described through the senses and the sense bank; only metaphor is keyed, to the POV's own life (R48-04). No culture decides what gets noticed.
options.sample: The hall was cold and dim, and Tobias Kell stood where the steward had left him while his eyes caught up. Lamps burned low along the walls. The floor was bare stone, swept. At the far end a dais held a low table and nothing else. Somewhere behind a screen a man was cutting wood with a small knife, a scratch and a pause and a scratch. The steward came back, bowed from the waist, and said the lord would see him after the bread.

options.label: The viewer's culture decides
options.consequence: The POV notices what his culture's eye catches wherever he stands: an Accord clerk prices a Moto hall, a Kharven rider counts its fuel. Each Inventory gains a 'Notices first' line.
options.sample: Tobias Kell priced the hall before his eyes had finished adjusting. There was no meter by the door, so the lamps burned oil, and dear oil by the smell, the sort an Accord house would have metered and billed by the quarter. The lacquer on the dais was a clerk's wages for a year. No board hung anywhere, no seal, no register in sight, and that troubled him more than the cold. Nothing said in a room with nothing written in it would ever be entered. The steward bowed and told him to wait for the bread.

options.label: The place's culture decides
options.consequence: A place is described through the eye of the culture that built it, whoever enters: a Moto hall reads through shadow, lacquer and silence. Each Inventory gains a 'Notices first' line.
options.sample: The hall kept its light low on purpose. Lacquer on the dais was a red so dark it read black until a lamp guttered, and then a seam of garnet ran along its edge and went out. Fourteen scratches stood in the doorpost at hand height, the oldest worn smooth by thumbs. The stone floor had been swept twice. One carved bird sat in a niche, serving no purpose Tobias Kell could find. The steward bowed once from the waist, the cloth of his sleeves moving and nothing else, and left him a silence to fill.

options.label: Place supplies, viewer judges
options.consequence: The place's Inventory sets what is in the room; the POV's culture sets what he makes of it, misreadings included. Each Inventory gains a 'Notices first' line for both jobs.
options.sample: Lacquer on the dais was a red so dark it read black until a lamp guttered, and Tobias Kell's first thought was what it had cost. Fourteen scratches stood in the doorpost at hand height. He took them for a tally of debts and looked along the walls for the register that matched them, and found none. One carved bird sat in a niche doing nothing at all, which any Accord house would long since have sold. The steward bowed and left him a silence. Kell filled it by counting the lamps.

questions.rec_reason: The place supplies the subjects and the outsider supplies the misreading, which characterises both cultures in one pass and sits well with folk beliefs left uncorrected (R53-15).

questions.title: New Standing Inventory fields
questions.question: Which new fields should every Standing Inventory gain, so description has something to draw on across the range?
questions.context: R6-8 fixed the Inventory at nine categories (food, greeting, oaths, time, the dead, objects, exchange, proverbs, body); later rulings added senses, Gone, folk beliefs and literacy. Nothing supplies land, building, dress, living things, music or law, so description keeps reaching for what is there. New fields are drafted from the wiki and looked up, never invented (R53-29).

options.label: Land, sky and season
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains terrain and climate, the sky as the culture names it, and its seasons with their signs.

options.label: Building and dress
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains architecture and ornament, the house plan, and dress by rank: cloth, cut, colour, adornment and worn scent.

options.label: Living things and play
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains what grows, what is kept, hunted and feared, and its music, games, toys and one or two festivals.

options.label: Law, travel, more senses
options.consequence: Each Inventory gains law and punishment (R53-11), succession (R60-21), roads, vehicles and inns, and Temperature and Motion beside the five senses.

questions.rec_reason: Range needs supply: without these fields every culture keeps being described through what it eats, swears and owns. Each culture's new fields are drafted when that culture next reaches the page.

questions.title: Craft and labour on the page
questions.question: When a craft or trade is on the page, how much of the work itself gets described?
questions.context: R6-5 keeps 'rust, weathering, wear, labour' described in full and R12-6 gives a rite 'an order of operations', but in the archive crafts are named more than shown and finished work is never looked at for its quality. O'Brian and the Japanese master-craftsman story give the work step by step; wabi-sabi (the beauty of the worn and imperfect) looks at what it made.

options.label: Named when used (current)
options.consequence: Crafts appear when the plot uses them and pass in a line or two. Nothing new is required.
options.sample: The carver cut the ward into the new doorpost while the courier watered his horse, and by the time the horse had drunk it was done. The groove showed nothing; Ketsuen wards never do. He wiped sap off the chisel on his thigh, tapped the post once with the mallet handle, listened, and nodded. The courier paid him in dried fish and rode on before the light went.

options.label: Shown as process
options.consequence: Whenever a craft is on the page, at least one stretch runs as process: tool, material and steps in order, with the worker's body doing them.
options.sample: The carver laid his palm flat on the cedar and left it there until the sap under the bark stopped feeling cold. Then he scored the outline with an awl, shallow, along the grain. The chisel went in at the top of each stroke and came out at the bottom, three passes to a stroke, each deeper than the last, and he blew the chips clear between them. Sap rose in the cut and he let it rise. When the last groove was done he tapped the post with the mallet handle and listened to the note it gave back.

options.label: Process and its beauty
options.consequence: Process as in B, and the finished thing is looked at for its quality: what good work looks like in that craft, through the POV's eye.
options.sample: He scored the outline with an awl and cut each stroke in three passes, blowing the chips clear, and when he stepped back the courier understood why people walked a day to see the old wards at the stone gate. The grooves ran with the grain so cleanly the glyph seemed to have grown in the wood. Sap welled in the deepest stroke and hung there, amber on pale timber. There was no colour in it and no ornament. A Ketsuen ward shows nothing, and this one showed nothing perfectly.

options.label: Full craft set piece
options.consequence: Once per arc a craft gets a full passage at set-piece length: choosing tools, judging material, each step, the risks, the finished thing and its price.
options.sample: He chose the chisel by its handle, the one worn dark where his thumb went, and stropped it on his boot. Then the awl, and a pot of lamp-black for the line, because his teacher had never let him trust the eye on green timber. The cedar had to be wet enough to take a clean groove and dry enough not to tear. He pressed a thumbnail into the post, judged it, and sat down on his kit to wait for the sun to come off the wood. A ward cut in a warm post wanders.

questions.rec_reason: It fills the gap the archive shows most clearly, the beauty of finished work, and the Japanese and Western craft traditions meet in it; a full set piece stays available when a craft is the plot.

questions.title: The table
questions.question: When a meal is on the page, what of it gets described?
questions.context: Food is named in the archive and rarely tasted (about 1.5 mentions per 1,000 words), and table customs appear as a line. Dream of the Red Chamber spends pages on dishes and seating; Martin lists a feast course by course; Japanese prose gives a small portion and its vessel full attention. WOTR tables already carry laws: the skin at a Kharven door, the Moto host's three days.

options.label: Named, as now
options.consequence: Meals and customs appear as a line: what was served and who ate first. The archive's current habit.
options.sample: At the door the woman held out the skin and the courier drank, because every Hallenfeld man who rode north was warned what it meant to refuse it. Inside there was broth and windmeat and a place on the bench by the fire. He ate what he was given. The old man in the corner had the first bowl. The courier had the third, and was glad of it.

options.label: Tasted in the mouth
options.consequence: Every meal on the page gets taste: what the food does in the mouth, its heat, fat and sourness, how long it chews. The order of serving stays a line.
options.sample: The skin came first, at the door. It was sour and faintly fizzing, and it left a film on his teeth that tasted of yeast and the inside of a seal. The broth after it had the fat still floating, so hot it took the skin off the roof of his mouth, and he kept drinking. The windmeat was hard as bark until it softened, and it gave up salt and game slowly, a little more the longer he chewed.

options.label: Served in its order
options.consequence: The table is shown as a rite: who is served first and by whom, from what vessel, who eats last, and what goes unsaid about it. Taste stays a line.
options.sample: The woman met him on the step with the skin unstoppered and did not move until he had drunk. She took it back without wiping the mouth. Inside, the bowls came off the hearth in their order: the first to her husband's father, whose hands had gone in the Thin Weeks and who was fed by the youngest girl; the second to her husband; the third to the courier. She ate last, standing, from the bottom of the pot, and nobody remarked on it.

options.label: Order and taste both
options.consequence: The order of serving and the taste in the mouth are both on the page whenever a meal is.
options.sample: The woman held the skin out on the step until he drank; it was sour and fizzing and it coated his teeth with yeast. Inside, the bowls came off the hearth in their order. The first went to her husband's father, whose hands had gone in the Thin Weeks, and the youngest girl fed him. The second went to her husband, the third to the courier: broth with the fat still floating, hot enough to scald, salt and marrow under the scorch. She ate last, standing, from the bottom of the pot.

questions.rec_reason: The order of serving is the cheapest way to show who matters in a house, and taste is the sense the archive uses least; WOTR's tables already have the laws to fill both.

questions.title: Landscape and sky
questions.question: How much of the land and the sky does an outdoor scene describe?
questions.context: R53-09 shows 'the actual weather' in every outdoor scene and R49-22 keeps the world 'described, not personified'; past that, the archive sees landscape through windows and the sky almost never. Chinese shanshui builds a view in far, middle and near planes with the person small; Tolkien gives the road its miles and slope; canon already names the moon, five wanderers and the Nail.

options.label: Weather and near ground (current)
options.consequence: The actual weather (R53-09) and the ground near the POV; wider land and sky only when the plot needs them.
options.sample: The snow had stopped by the time they topped the ridge, and the cold came down hard behind it. The scout reined in. Below, the Seat's walls showed darker grey on the grey rock, with lamps in the gatehouse and smoke standing over the outer town. The courier's horse blew and stamped. He had lost the feeling in his face an hour back. "Keep to the ruts," the scout said. "They're frozen hard enough to ring."

options.label: One wide view outdoors
options.consequence: Every outdoor scene gets one wide view built far, middle and near, with the people small in it, and the sky in it after dark.
options.sample: From the ridge the whole north lay open. Far out, the plain ran white and level to a line of low black hills, and over them the aurora hung in two green folds. Nearer, the rock rose grey and the Seat sat on it, its old courses darker than the new stone above. Nearer still, the outer town's stacks put their smoke straight up into the still air. On the ridge two horses stood blowing, and the courier, very small against all of it, could not feel his face.

options.label: Land as route
options.consequence: Travel ground is described as route: distance, slope, footing, what the road is made of, and the time it takes at a walk (R53-08 rates).
options.sample: The last nine miles had taken the light. A mile out the road came off the moss plain onto bare rock, and the ruts there were frozen hard enough to ring under the hooves; the scout kept the horses on the crown of the road, where the ice lay thinnest. From the ridge it ran downhill all the way, a long slope of wind-scoured stone with the Seat at the foot of it and the outer town's smoke marking where the ground flattened. Two hours at a walk, the scout said, if the grey held up.

options.label: The sky every night
options.consequence: Every night scene names the sky: the moon's phase (Shiro, the Lamp), which wanderers are up, the Nail, the aurora, and what people read in them.
options.sample: The Lamp stood a hand above the black hills, a night past full, and behind the Seat the aurora moved in two green folds without a sound. The Nail held still at the top of the sky where it always held. Low in the south the Red Ox showed dull and reddish, and the scout pointed it out with his whip and said nobody sane started a war while it went backwards. Under all that light the Seat was a grey rock with a few lamps on it, and the courier's breath stood white in front of his face.

questions.rec_reason: One wide view per outdoor scene is the clearest Eastern gain on the page and fills the thinnest gap; the sky comes into it after dark, and the route stays available whenever the road matters.

questions.title: Bodies after first sight
questions.question: Once a person has had their first-sight inventory, how is their body described when they come back?
questions.context: R49-28 gives everyone 'the full physical inventory all at first sight'; after that the archive's bodies are mostly hands. Abercrombie and Mantel keep a body changing under wear; Mishima and the cultivation novel dwell on a body's beauty; Holmes reads a life off a frame. The Ledger already carries injury and exhaustion from scene to scene.

options.label: When the plot needs (current)
options.consequence: After the first-sight inventory, a body comes back on the page only when the action uses it: a hand, a limp, a wound.
options.sample: The horse-master was at the lines again before light, forking hay with his back to the wind. He nodded when the courier came out. "Your grey's lame," he said. "Near fore. Stone bruise, likely." He bent, took the hoof between his knees, and showed the courier the sole, where a dark bloom of blood sat under the horn. "Three days off it," he said. "Four if you want her to carry you home."

options.label: One changed detail each time
options.consequence: Every return of a person carries one detail of what the body has changed since: a new wound, weight, fatigue, cold damage, a missed shave. The Ledger's costs show.
options.sample: The horse-master was at the lines again before light. Something had gone in his back since yesterday; he forked the hay from the hip in short strokes, and straightened in two stages with a hand on the post. Frost had got into the cracks of his knuckles in the night, and they had bled and dried black. He had not shaved. "Your grey's lame," he said. "Near fore." When he bent to take the hoof he did it slowly, and breathed out hard through his nose before he looked.

options.label: Beauty licensed
options.consequence: Any POV may dwell on a body as something to look at, man or woman, young or old, at length, in the terms of his own life.
options.sample: In the blue hour before light the horse-master's face had the colour and grain of old harness, every crease in it laid down by weather and kept supple with grease. He worked bare-forearmed in the cold, and the long muscle along the bone ran clean under the skin each time he lifted the fork, rope through a greased block. The courier had come out to see to his grey and stood watching longer than he meant to. "Your grey's lame," the horse-master said, without turning. "Near fore."

options.label: The body as a record
options.consequence: A returning person's body is read like a document: trade, age, old injuries and habits read off the frame by any POV with the eye for it.
options.sample: By daylight the courier could read the horse-master's life off him. A rider once: the knees bowed, the inside of each calf worn hairless by the saddle. Thirty winters of forking hay had built the right shoulder higher than the left. Two fingers on the bridle hand had set crooked after some old kick, and the frost-scars on both cheeks were waxy white and old, the kind one bad night leaves. "Your grey's lame," he said. "Near fore."

questions.rec_reason: It keeps every body under the Ledger's cost, one changed detail at a time, which is grimdark's strength; beauty and the read-a-life eye stay open to any POV whose life gives him them.

questions.title: Objects: price, grade, provenance
questions.question: When a notable object is on the page, how much of its value and history gets described?
questions.context: R46-2 names the item Tiers (Plain, Marked, Proofed and up) and the approved price table sets real prices, but objects on the page are seldom priced or traced. Balzac prices everything; cultivation novels grade a treasure by age and class; LitRPG gives every item a tooltip (a small panel of facts). The boxed item card is asked in the LitRPG section; this is the prose.

options.label: As the POV notices (current)
options.consequence: Objects carry what the POV would notice: wear, weight, a stamp. Price and history appear when the plot needs them.
options.sample: The dealer laid the sword on a fold of green baize and stepped back from it. It was an officer's blade, plain-hilted, the grip rewound in black cord, and when the buyer drew it a few inches the steel came out quiet and grey. Under his thumb at the ricasso were raised letters. The dealer named a price and did not look away while he named it.

options.label: Price whenever money moves
options.consequence: Every purchase, sale or bargain on the page names the price in the culture's money, quoted from the approved price table.
options.sample: The dealer laid the sword on a fold of green baize. Six gold, he said, and the buyer, who had paid eighteen for the horse tied outside, did the sum in his head and disliked it. A trooper's sabre on the next rack was ticketed at eight silver. He drew the blade a few inches. Under his thumb at the ricasso were raised letters, and the dealer said six gold again, as if it were the letters he was selling.

options.label: Full appraisal in prose
options.consequence: A notable object gets one passage giving maker, Tier by name, provenance and price, sourced from the price table and R46-2, through an appraising eye.
options.sample: "Proofed," the dealer said, and turned the blade to the lamp so the buyer could see the stamp at the ricasso: PROB EST in raised letters, and under it the proof-house's quarter punch, struck once and clean. Stannvaard steel, by the grain in the flat. Two owners. The first had it made for his commission; the second died of a fever with it on his hip, and the edge had never been reground. Six gold, the dealer said, the price of a Proofed blade with a clean history, and he would take nothing off for the worn cord.

options.label: Its life and lineage
options.consequence: A notable object is described through who made, carried, mended and died with it; price and Tier stay off the page unless asked.
options.sample: The sword had passed through three pairs of hands before it reached the dealer's baize. A captain of the Fourth had it made, and the pommel still carried his initials, half worn away by a palm. His son had it reground after a bad notch, and the new bevel caught the lamp a shade brighter than the old one near the guard. The third owner had rewound the grip in black cord and died with it in his hand. The buyer drew it a few inches and could feel all three of them in the balance.

questions.rec_reason: Appraisal is where the three traditions meet in one passage: Victorian price, Eastern grade and provenance, and the LitRPG item's legibility, kept in prose and sourced from the price table and the Tier names.

questions.title: Repetition against novelty
questions.question: How should description balance a culture's recurring signature items against new subjects?
questions.context: R6-9 reads 'Identity is repetition. Novelty is its enemy.', R51-31 sends scenes to the sense bank first, and R53-19 asks two signature items per culture per session. The archive shows the cost: repeated key-rings, stained fingers and closing lines. Homeric and pansori refrains make repetition carry identity; your 'wide variety of things' pulls the other way.

options.label: Recurrence first (current)
options.consequence: Scenes draw on the Inventory and sense bank first, with two signature items per culture per session (R53-19); invention is logged and secondary.
options.sample: The household sat down when the woodpile had been counted and the count called through the door. Somebody asked the courier how his stack was, and laughed when he had no answer. The night-stone sat warm at the edge of the hearth, where the fire had been. The old man said the boy who had gone to the Hallenfeld road was wet wood, and the woman told him to hush. Outside, the Thin Weeks were coming; everybody said so, and nobody said it twice.

options.label: Recur, and add one
options.consequence: R53-19's two signature items stay; R6-9's 'Novelty is its enemy' is rewritten so every scene also adds one subject the thread has not described, logged as canon (R53-21).
options.sample: The household sat down when the woodpile had been counted and the count called through the door. The night-stone sat warm at the hearth's edge. The two youngest had a game the courier had never seen: five knucklebones from a seal's flipper, tossed and caught on the back of the hand, the loser fetching snow for the pot. The girl won three times running and made her brother fetch it in his bare hands. The old man called him wet wood, and he went anyway.

options.label: Novelty first
options.consequence: The Inventory becomes a floor: Natalie invents texture freely and logs it, the quota drops to one signature item, and R6-9 is struck.
options.sample: The household sat down to a supper the courier had not met before: seal liver sliced thin and eaten frozen, with a pinch of salt on each piece. A bone flute lay on the shelf, three holes, and when the old man had eaten he played a tune on it with no ending, round and round, while the girls plaited horsehair into rope for the spring. The dogs had been let in for the night and lay against the door in a heap, steaming. Nobody counted anything.

options.label: Recur, changed each time
options.consequence: Signature items keep coming back, and each return shows how they have changed since the last: the woodpile lower, the stone cooler, the insult quieter.
options.sample: The woodpile had been counted again and the count called through the door, and it was lower than the night before by more than one night's burning. The night-stone at the hearth's edge was cooler under the woman's palm than it had been yesterday; they were banking the fire earlier. The old man called the absent boy wet wood again, more quietly. Nobody mentioned the Thin Weeks, which was new, and the courier had stayed long enough to mark it.

questions.rec_reason: Signature items keep a culture recognisable and the quota stays; each scene also adds one thing nobody has described yet, logged under R53-21, so the world widens as it repeats.

sections.title: How much and where
sections.intro: How much description a page carries, where it sits, who and what gets the full inventory, and how any of it is checked. Live law says lush throughout and a full inventory at first sight; these questions decide whether that holds in every mode.

questions.title: Overall density
questions.question: How dense should description run by default?
questions.context: This reopens R48-02 ('Lush throughout'), ruled 2026-09-26. Chinese baimiao (plain line drawing: a subject caught in one or two exact strokes) and Japanese ellipsis run spare; web serials and LitRPG run light and fast; Victorian and Martin-style prose run dense. Your new ask is about width, which density alone does not settle.

options.label: Lush throughout (current)
options.consequence: R48-02 stands: full sensory layering in every scene, slower and denser. The blend widens what is described and keeps the amount.
options.sample: The gauge-house at the end of Tallow Row held the smell of lamp oil and brass polish, and under both, damp iron from the standpipe in the corner, which wept a slow bead at its cap. It was the maintenance hour, a little after three, and the district's hum had dropped to the low note it kept while the Board ran its checks. Mary Coyle hung her coat on the bronze reach by the door. The slate behind the gauge glass was chalked with yesterday's readings in the inspector's square hand, and the needle sat just off the stop, trembling.

options.label: Spare base, lush peaks
options.consequence: R48-02 is rewritten: one exact stroke per beat in talk, travel and routine work; full layering at arrivals that matter, quiet scenes, set pieces and aftermaths.
options.sample: Mary Coyle let herself into the gauge-house at the maintenance hour and hung her coat on the bronze reach. Lamp oil, brass polish. She lit the lamp and read the needle. It sat just off the stop, where it always sat at this hour, and it was trembling, and in nine years she had never once seen it tremble.

options.label: Light, web-serial pace
options.consequence: R48-02 is repealed: one or two details per beat, short paragraphs, the weight carried by action and dialogue, as web serials and LitRPG read.
options.sample: Mary Coyle unlocked the gauge-house a little after three and hung her coat on its hook. Lamp lit. Kettle on. She had done this for nine years and could have done it asleep. Then she looked at the needle and stopped with the match still burning in her fingers. It was trembling. "That's wrong," she said, to nobody, and reached for the book.

options.label: Set by the POV's culture
options.consequence: Density follows the POV's culture: Moto and Yukari spare, Accord and Stannvaard dense with figures and seals, Kharven counted. Each Inventory gains a density line.
options.sample: Mary Coyle entered the gauge-house at fourteen counts past the third hour by the wire clock and signed the book under the inspector's seal, green wax, unbroken. Standpipe capped, one bead weeping at the cap. Lamp oil a third down the reservoir. Six readings on the slate from yesterday, each initialled in the square hand. The needle sat just off the stop, correct for the hour. It trembled. She entered that too, with the count, before she let herself think about what it was.

questions.rec_reason: You ruled lush a week ago and the new ask is width; widening what lush description covers delivers the blend, and the spare Eastern eye still reaches the page through culture-keyed noticing.

questions.title: Where description sits
questions.question: Where in a scene should the larger descriptive passages sit?
questions.context: Today texture is woven through every beat (R53-30) and arrivals open on the senses (R49-25). Western modern prose weaves; the Victorian novel front-loads the room; Japanese ma (the meaningful pause) and the wuxia held moment pool description in a lull; Gu Long and the sword film hold it for the aftermath. Placement decides what the reader is looking at while the news lands.

options.label: Woven through (current)
options.consequence: Texture runs through every beat (R53-30) and arrivals open on the senses (R49-25). No passage is held back for a pause.
options.sample: The messenger came in with snow still on his shoulders and went to one knee on the swept stone, and the steward let him kneel there while the lamp by the door finished guttering. "The Shirogane envoy turned back at the pass," the messenger said. Melt ran off his collar and dotted the floor. The steward's hand went to his sash and stayed there. Behind the screen the knife that had been cutting at wood all morning stopped. "Turned back," the steward said. "Or was sent back."

options.label: Front-loaded
options.consequence: The place gets its full description at the entrance and threshold; after that the scene runs on action and talk with single details.
options.sample: The audience hall kept its light low: oil lamps along the walls, lacquer on the dais so dark a red it read black, fourteen scratches in the doorpost worn smooth at the bottom, a stone floor swept twice and cold enough to ache through a boot. A knife scratched at wood behind a screen. The messenger came in and knelt. "The Shirogane envoy turned back at the pass." The steward looked at him. "Turned back," he said. "Or was sent back." "I don't know." "Then find out."

options.label: Woven, pooling in lulls
options.consequence: Texture stays woven through every beat; the longer passages are held for pauses, silences and aftermaths, so the news lands bare and the room is seen in the quiet after.
options.sample: The messenger came in with snow on his shoulders, knelt, and said it. "The Shirogane envoy turned back at the pass." Nobody answered him. In the quiet the lamp by the door guttered and steadied, and melt ran off his collar and dotted the swept stone in a line toward the dais. Behind the screen the knife that had been cutting at wood all morning had stopped. The lacquer on the dais held one seam of garnet where the lamp found it. The steward let the silence run until the messenger's knee began to shake. "Turned back," he said. "Or was sent back."

options.label: Held for the aftermath
options.consequence: While the beat runs, description is bare; when it is over, the scene looks at what is left. Sword-film and Gu Long pacing.
options.sample: The messenger came in, knelt, and said it: the Shirogane envoy had turned back at the pass. The steward asked whether turned or sent. The messenger did not know. He was told to find out, and went. Afterwards the hall kept the marks of it. Melt from his collar lay in a dotted line from the door to the dais. The lamp by the door had guttered out and nobody relit it. Behind the screen the knife had stopped cutting, and the bird it had been making sat half-finished on the bench, one wing still in the wood.

questions.rec_reason: Woven texture keeps the immersion you ruled for, and letting the larger passages pool in pauses and aftermaths gives the page Japanese ma and the wuxia held moment without slowing the action.

questions.title: Who gets the full inventory
questions.question: Which people, places and things get the full first-sight inventory?
questions.context: R49-28 and Table Rule 11 give a person the full inventory (hair by comparison, face, body by area, clothes, marks) at first sight; places, rooms, creatures and objects have no such rule. Chinese baimiao catches a minor figure in one stroke; cultivation novels and the gothic give a sect ground or a castle a full entrance. Every inventory costs words in a 3,500-word turn.

options.label: People only (current)
options.consequence: Every person gets the full inventory at first sight; places and things get what the scene needs.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat with a brazier in it. The sergeant who stepped out to meet him had hair the grey of old felt, cropped to the skull, and a broad flat face burned dark across the cheekbones by the wind. He was short and heavy through the chest and belly, bandy in the leg, a rider gone to ground. His hide-coat had been patched at both elbows with sealskin and greased black at the cuffs. A white frost-scar crossed the bridge of his nose. He held out his hand for the papers without a word.

options.label: People, places, creatures, objects
options.consequence: Every person, place, room, creature and significant object gets a full inventory at first sight, each in one passage.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat two horses wide, the old dark courses at its foot and new grey stone above, an iron grate overhead with its teeth rimed white, a brazier of seal fat smoking in a niche and a bench worn hollow by sitting. The sergeant who came out of it had hair the grey of old felt, cropped close, and a flat face burned dark across the cheekbones. He was short and heavy, bandy from the saddle, his hide-coat patched with sealskin at the elbows. A frost-scar whitened his nose. He held out his hand for the papers.

options.label: Major full, minor one stroke
options.consequence: Major people keep the full inventory; minor people (a role until they speak twice or matter, R50-27) get one exact stroke. Places stay as now.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat with a brazier in it. A sergeant came out, bandy-legged, a frost-scar white across his nose, and held out his hand for the papers without a word. He read them upside down, which told the courier he could not read at all, and handed them back. "Go up," he said. "Lead the horse. The ruts will break her legs."

options.label: Places full, minors one stroke
options.consequence: Major people, places, rooms, creatures and significant objects get the full inventory; minor people get one exact stroke.
options.sample: The gatehouse was a stone throat two horses wide, the old dark courses at its foot and new grey stone above them, an iron grate overhead with its teeth rimed white. A brazier of seal fat smoked in a niche beside a bench worn hollow by forty years of sitting, and the walls were black with smoke to the height of a man's head. A sergeant came out, bandy-legged, a frost-scar white across his nose, and held out his hand for the papers. He read them upside down and gave them back.

questions.rec_reason: Places and creatures earn the full entrance the cultivation and gothic traditions give them, and one-stroke minor people end the identity-card sameness the archive shows; major people keep the full inventory.

questions.title: The order of a first inventory
questions.question: In what order should a first-sight inventory of a person run?
questions.context: Table Rule 11 sets the order: hair by comparison, face, body, clothes, marks, then want and voice. The archive runs it the same way every time, and introductions read like identity cards. The modern Western novel feeds a person in pieces as they act; the Japanese war tale starts a fighter at his armour; a culture-keyed eye starts where its culture looks.

options.label: Fixed order (current)
options.consequence: Table Rule 11's order stands: hair by comparison, face, body by area, clothes, marks, then want and voice, in one passage.
options.sample: The Reckoner's hair was the flat unlit white of old bone, bound back in one black cord. Her face was long and narrow, grey-violet as a four-day bruise, the eyes set deep under a heavy brow. She was tall and spare through the shoulders and hips, and she carried her weight high, like a heron. Her coat was salt-black and cut close, the cuffs shiny with wear. A callus stood on the side of her right forefinger, yellow and hard. She showed both hands open as she came in.

options.label: The POV's order
options.consequence: The inventory stays one passage at first sight but runs in the order this POV would look: a clerk prices first, a surgeon reads wounds first, a rider looks at hands.
options.sample: He priced her coat before he looked at her face: salt-black, close-cut, good cloth kept long, the cuffs gone shiny. Then her hands, shown open as she came in, a callus on the right forefinger yellow and hard where a nib had ridden for thirty years, and no ink anywhere on them, so a careful one. The face came last, because it was worth least to him: long and narrow, grey-violet as a four-day bruise, under hair the flat white of old bone, bound in one black cord.

options.label: In pieces, in motion
options.consequence: R49-28's 'in one descriptive passage' is repealed for people: the full inventory arrives in pieces over the first page as the person acts.
options.sample: The Reckoner came in showing both hands open and sat without being asked. When she reached for the ruled leaf the clerk saw the callus on her forefinger, hard and yellow. She read with her head tipped back, which put the lamp on her face: long, narrow, grey-violet as a four-day bruise. Halfway down the page she pulled the black cord from her hair, retied it tighter over the flat white, and kept reading. Her coat creaked at the shoulder when she turned the leaf; salt-black, cut close, shiny at the cuffs.

options.label: Their culture's order
options.consequence: The inventory runs in the order the described person's culture presents itself: Korvaeth hands first, Moto eyes first, Accord token first.
options.sample: Her hands came first, as a Korvaeth's do: shown open at the door, palms out, then turned, to show there was nothing in them and a callus on the right forefinger hard as horn. Then the cord, one black cord binding the flat white hair, wound in nine tight passes. Then she stood still and let him look, and that was the face: long and narrow, grey-violet as a four-day bruise. Her coat, salt-black and close-cut, he took in only when she sat.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps your full inventory in one passage and ends the identity-card sameness, and the order itself characterises the POV: an Accord clerk prices the coat before he sees the face.

questions.title: Catalogue or telling detail
questions.question: When should description run as a long catalogue, and when as a single telling detail?
questions.context: No rule governs the long list. Homer's catalogue of ships, Malory's arming, the Japanese war tale's armour list, the Chinese chapter novel's battle array and the LitRPG inventory all make length the point; Chekhov and Chinese baimiao trust one telling detail. Lambert already falls into inventory under stress (R52-16).

options.label: By ear (current)
options.consequence: No rule; lush layering decides, and lists appear when the moment seems to want one.
options.sample: The rider armed in the yard with the wall above him. He belted the hide-coat tight, pulled the mail over it, and settled the iron cap with its fur lining down over his ears. His breath stood white. The sword went on the left hip, the knife at the small of his back. A boy held the horse. When he was done he grunted, took the reins and swung up, and the frozen ground rang under the hooves as the horse turned.

options.label: Catalogue at set occasions
options.consequence: Arming, feasts, markets, musters, treasuries and loot may run as full catalogues; elsewhere description stays woven. The chain ceiling still holds, so a catalogue rides on semicolons.
options.sample: He armed in the yard, piece by piece, and the boy handed each piece up: the quilted under-shirt, gone stiff with old sweat; the hide-coat, greased black at the cuffs; the mail shirt, rebound at the left hip in new lacing; the belt worn shiny where his hand went to it; the iron cap lined with fox fur; the mittens on a cord through both sleeves; the sabre, Hallenfeld steel bought with two winters' salt; the knife; the horn cup; the twist of windmeat for the wall. Last the horse, a grey with a torn ear, who blew at him.

options.label: Telling detail, rare lists
options.consequence: One exact detail is the default; a catalogue is allowed at most once per scene, and kept short.
options.sample: He armed in the yard without hurry, and the only thing the boy remembered after was the mittens: threaded on a cord through both sleeves of the hide-coat, the way his mother had done them when he was small, so he could not lose them on the wall. He swung up. The frozen ground rang under the hooves, and he did not look back at the yard.

options.label: Catalogue by culture
options.consequence: Counting cultures (Kharven, Korvaeth, Accord, Dawi) catalogue in counts; cultures of restraint (Moto, Yukari, Eresse) give the one detail.
options.sample: He counted it on as he armed, as every Kharven counts what he carries north: one under-shirt, one hide-coat, one mail shirt rebound at the hip, one belt, one cap with fox fur, two mittens on one cord, one sabre, one knife, one horn cup, three twists of windmeat, a day and a half of eating or a week of going short. The boy counted with him under his breath. They came to the same number, and he swung up.

questions.rec_reason: The catalogue is shared ground for Homer, the war tale, the chapter novel and LitRPG, and tying it to set occasions keeps it from swallowing ordinary scenes.

questions.title: Description inside a fight
questions.question: How much of the place and the watchers is described while a fight is running?
questions.context: R48-33 traces every exchange and R53-30 still asks one world-only detail per beat, fights included; in practice fights carry body and mechanism and little else. Wuxia and Homer hold a frozen instant mid-battle; chanbara (the Japanese sword-fight film) runs the exchange bare and spends its stillness before and after. Choreography itself is the combat section's question.

options.label: Body and mechanism (current)
options.consequence: Inside a fight, description stays on bodies, blades and the mechanism of the hit; the setting returns when the fight ends.
options.sample: The Shirogane man came into measure on the sergeant's left, and the sergeant cut from the shoulder too early. The Shirogane blade met his in the bind, rode down it, and took him across the back of the forearm as he tried to recover. The tendons parted. His fingers opened and the sabre turned in his hand and dropped. Blood came in pulses down the inside of his wrist, bright in the cold, and he stepped back holding the arm against his chest.

options.label: The room keeps living
options.consequence: Every exchange carries one detail of the place going on around it: snow, a sound, a watcher, the light. R53-30 applied inside fights.
options.sample: The Shirogane man came into measure on the sergeant's left, the snow squeaking under him, and the sergeant cut from the shoulder too early. Along the gallery rail a line of riders leaned out, breath standing white. The blades met in the bind; the Shirogane edge rode down and took the sergeant across the back of the forearm, and the tendons parted. Behind the wall an axe kept splitting rounds, steady, as if nothing were happening in the yard. The sabre dropped. Blood ran bright down the sergeant's wrist and steamed where it hit the snow.

options.label: Held instant, then outcome
options.consequence: Exchanges run traced and lean; at the deciding moment the page holds still for a passage of setting before the outcome lands.
options.sample: They came together once and parted, and for a moment nothing in the yard moved. The sergeant stood with his sabre still high. Snow had begun again, fine as flour, settling on the Shirogane man's shoulders and on the black lacquer of his scabbard. A rider on the gallery had his cup halfway to his mouth. The axe behind the wall had stopped. Then the sergeant's fingers opened, the sabre turned in his hand and fell, and the blood came down the inside of his wrist in pulses, bright, steaming where it struck.

options.label: Bare inside, full around
options.consequence: The exchange itself runs bare; the full description of the place sits before the first cut and after the last.
options.sample: The Shirogane man came into measure. The sergeant cut early. Bind, slide, the edge across the back of the forearm, and the sabre was on the ground. Afterwards the yard took it in. A line of riders stood along the gallery rail with their breath hanging. The axe behind the wall had stopped. Blood ran down the sergeant's wrist in pulses and steamed in the snow, and the Shirogane man flicked his blade once, so that a line of red dots crossed the white, and sheathed it with a small sound.

questions.rec_reason: A held instant at the deciding exchange gives the blend the wuxia and Homeric pause, keeps the traced exchange clean, and gives R53-30's world detail somewhere to live in a fight.

questions.title: Pacing in turns and written scenes
questions.question: How should description be paced in a roleplay turn, against a written scene?
questions.context: R48-28 and R49-30 make every reply a turn of about 3,500 words, and R49-29 fills it 'about half texture and talk, half the world moving'. Web serials front-load and then run; the Victorian serial spreads description through the instalment. The range rule in DS1 needs a shape that works turn by turn without bloating a turn.

options.label: Same law both (current)
options.consequence: Turns and written scenes follow the same density and placement law, and R49-29's half-and-half fill stands.

options.label: Turns open dense
options.consequence: A turn opens on its full texture (the place, the new thing in it), then the world moves to the stop in single details; written scenes spread description through.

options.label: One group deep per turn
options.consequence: Each turn takes its lead subject group deep and touches the rest lightly, the lead rotating turn to turn; written scenes range wide inside one scene.

options.label: Turns lighter, scenes lush
options.consequence: Roleplay turns run at a spare baseline so the world moves faster; written scenes and set pieces stay lush.

questions.rec_reason: It makes the range rule work at the table: each turn goes deep on one subject and the thread rotates, so a 3,500-word turn widens the world without becoming a survey.

questions.title: Checking the range
questions.question: How should the range and placement of description be checked?
questions.context: verify_scene counts subjects for one culture only: the Kharven signature items, when the Kharven culture flag is set (R49-54). R48-45 says 'every turn passes the full checker', and the Stop hook blocks a reply on any FAIL. Keyword counts are rough: 'seal' catches wax and animal alike, so a census of subject groups will misfire sometimes.

options.label: By ear, no check
options.consequence: Nothing is counted; range rests on Natalie's judgement and your reading.

options.label: Brief and session count
options.consequence: scene_brief names the lead and supporting groups before drafting; session_end lists groups untouched for four scenes. verify_scene is unchanged.

options.label: Census as a WARN
options.consequence: verify_scene gains keyword lists per subject group and WARNs when a scene touches too few groups or one group takes over half; the brief and session count from B also run.

options.label: Census as a FAIL
options.consequence: The same census FAILs, so the Stop hook blocks a reply that misses the range until it is fixed.

questions.rec_reason: Keyword counts are rough, so they should ask for a read and never block a reply; the session count catches drift across a thread, which is where sameness actually shows.

settled.point: Every outdoor scene shows the actual weather, tracked like a clock.
settled.why_not_asked: Live law already requires it, and every landscape option above builds on it.

settled.point: Every beat carries at least one detail that could only exist in this world.
settled.why_not_asked: Every tradition in the blend agrees with it; it is the floor any range rule stands on.

settled.point: A mixed room layers every culture present in roughly equal measure.
settled.why_not_asked: Culture-keyed noticing (DS6) works inside it; the blend gives no reason to change the measure.

settled.point: World facts are looked up and gaps flagged; a culture with no Inventory gets one drafted from the wiki before its scene.
settled.why_not_asked: New Inventory fields (DS7) and the missing Mahuo, Hon-guk, lineage-hall, chartered-household and tundra Inventories are drafted under these rules as each culture reaches the page.

settled.point: Texture invented in play is canon once logged.
settled.why_not_asked: Wider description needs exactly this licence, and it already stands.

settled.point: Wear, rust, weathering and labour are described in full.
settled.why_not_asked: It agrees with wabi-sabi and with the Victorian eye alike; DS8 builds on it.

settled.point: Travel and waiting pass in a line when nothing is at stake.
settled.why_not_asked: The range rules govern what is on the page; skipping dull stretches stays, and a route described in full (DS10) is for roads that matter.

settled.point: Real history is taken exactly and bent one step, and real cultures may be blended into one WOTR culture.
settled.why_not_asked: These already license Eastern and Western subjects alike in every Inventory.
